articles.title: Show HN: Hob - Open-source, on device alternative to Claude Cowork and ChatGPT
articles.snippet:
Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself.

Main features:

- Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows)

- Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.)

- Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG)

- MCP support

- Image recognition

- CRUD to your local filesystem

- Works fully offline with no internet

Before building this I tried every local AI app I could find, but it seemed each one had different problems. The main thing I noticed is that none of them could do what the ChatGPT and Claude apps do with your files, e.g. read and change files in a folder, look at images, run code in a sandbox, draw a chart. The most advanced thing any of them did was paste a plain text file into a small context window, which basically failed as soon as you had a file larger than a few KB. I couldn't find anything that could easily parse images and bigger PDFs.

The OSS solutions that were more advanced all seemed to default to hosted models (either OSS or closed), which defeats the entire point of the privacy that on-device OSS offers. They also seemed to push towards an account/open-core style business.

I build it using Electron bridged with llama.cpp in its own process. On initial load, the system will try and figure out if you have a compatible graphics card and if not default to CPU-only (I ran into a lot of issues of graphics card beeing seemingly compatible but then crashing on first query, there's a whole saga to this lol). Code execution happens in a sandbox that can only write to the chat's folder and has no network unless asked (sandbox-exec on macOS, Landlock on Linux and a low-integrity process on Windows). Images go to a small Qwen3-VL model. Dictation is a local Whisper model.

The hardest part was definitely to get the smaller models to use tools reliably. Ran into a ton of issues of 4B models happily saying "here's your chart" without ever calling the chart tool or get stuck in an infinite call loop. I spent a fair amount of the work building guards vs tweaking prompts (that didn't really work for small models).

I understand the pushback that local models are weaker than frontier cloud models. This is true, but for most tasks for most normal people, I'd argue you rarely need the newest frontier model. From my own evals, systems with 16+ GB of RAM do really well, and if you have a GPU or more RAM, you get very close to what you'll get out of the box with a frontier hosted model.

Excited to hear what you think and see how it runs on other systems!

articles.title: Sebastian Raschka's from-scratch video course on building reasoning models
articles.snippet: Build Your Own Reasoning Model: A Full Video Course Subscribe Sign in Building Reasoning Models from the Ground Up: A Full Video Course Eight videos and over 11 hours of coding, covering evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation in Python and PyTorch. Sebastian Raschka, PhD Oct 24, 2026 297 12 33 Share I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. articles.summaryKo: Sebastian Raschka가 추론 모델을 밑바닥부터 구현하는 8개 비디오, 총 11시간 분량의 코딩 강좌를 공개했다. Every week, a group of elderly birders spend hours hunkering down inside a wooden hide in the English countryside, peering through binoculars as they excitedly share what they spot. An oystercatcher's long, bright beak probing the pebbled ground; two great crested grebes bobbing in the water, their plumed heads poised. Most of these birdwatchers have difficulty recalling what happened earlier that day, and might struggle to follow a conversation. But they become animated when swapping notes on the birds that fill the sky around Forge Mill Lake in the UK's West Midlands. Among them is 78-year-old Harold*. He loved the outdoors when he was younger, but more recently dementia has made him withdrawn and anxious. His daughter Lucy* brought him here, hoping that the change of scenery and peaceful lake might be good for him. After an apprehensive start, Harold began smiling when someone pointed out a robin and enjoyed watching the ducks splashing in the water. Blue tits darted between the nearby trees, and Lucy saw Harold laugh for the first time in a long time. "For that moment in time he was present in the moment, he wasn't worried about his memory or his confidence. articles.title: CSS-Tricks has a new owner
articles.snippet: CSS-Tricks has a new owner! | CSS-Tricks Ad WordPress sites from those who know WordPress best. --> Skip to main content CSS-Tricks Since 2007 Articles Almanac Guides Links Newsletter Shop Account icon-account Search css-tricks news CSS-Tricks has a new owner! By Geoff Graham on Oct 26, 2026 NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. Ad --> This is pretty wild, but let’s get right to it because it’s big news: CSS-Tricks is an independent site once again! Just to recap: DigitalOcean purchased CSS-Tricks in 2022 from Chris Coyier, who founded the site in 2007. Chris ran it all the way up to that purchase. Here we are in 2026, and I’m taking independent ownership of the site. So, wait, who owns the site? That’d be me. (Wow, never imagined I would get to say that!) Of course, I have a small, awesome team to help with the day-to-day management of the site. That all said, I do envision that some things will change. In fact, I’m planning that they will change in what I hope are very good ways. Maybe a question-answer thing makes sense here since this is very much an evolving discussion. Do you, like, own the site now? Yes, I’ve got the keys to the castle, so to speak. And, even after 12 years of working on the site, I’ll admit I’m a little overwhelmed and nervous about that. I mean, it’s an investment for sure, as you can imagine, and I’m making this my full-time job. At least for a while. I want to make CSS-Tricks both a real community and a place that’s inclusive of everyone , no matter where they are in their front-end learning journey. That’s going to take some work and time. How can you afford this? My latest IPO launched, and I’m now worth one trillion dollars. Wait, wait. That’s not right. It’s going to be hard. Advertising will certainly be needed now. But, in order to keep the lights on, I’ll have to approach them differently. In the pre-DigitalOcean days we sold real ad packages with things like display ads, sponsored posts, newsletter sponsors, and the like. As an independent website, we will need to return to our advertising roots. So, if you’re in a place looking to advertise, please do reach out ! LOL, advertising. Right?! Ad revenue can’t be the only thing paying the bills. I have lots of ideas and several plates already spinning. Like, I’ve been neck deep in developing an HTML/CSS course for beginners. (And you can now support the site by becoming a member — thanks in advance!) LOL, courses. Educational content has been in the dumps lately, right? Again, I’m hoping that CSS-Tricks will be more inclusive, no matter where you or anyone else is at in the learning journey. This place has traditionally been for folks who know what they’re doing. But I’m truly committed to creating more entry points for those getting started, particularly as our field is in the early throes of a growing skills gap . And yes, I do believe that learning the basics is more important now than ever . But what learning actually looks like is what

articles.title: Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11
articles.snippet: Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11 · enlyth enlyth . posts tags rss Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11 26 October 2026 · 2 min read #windows #gui Early investigation For a while I’ve been wondering about a silly question, which is, what’s the oldest application with a GUI that will still run on Windows 11 without modifications or emulation. Given Windows’ excellent backwards compatibility, I expected the answer to be something impressively old. Sadly, Windows 11 can’t run 16-bit Windows programs by itself, because 64-bit Windows has no NTVDM , so we’re going to have to find something from the early NT era. I remember asking this question a while ago on an anonymous forum, where someone pointed me to Win32s , and suggested to find an early release version of it with FREECELL.exe . So I did exactly that, and lo and behold, FREECELL.EXE with a date modified of 22-Feb-93 running and fully playable, without any changes on the latest version of Windows 11: At the time of this post, that’s a 33 years and 8 months old application, which is impressively almost as old as me. So I kinda thought “cool”, considered this a solved mystery and forgot about it shortly afterwards. But for some reason, this question popped into my mind again lately and this time I decided to dig deeper to see if I can find something older. Further efforts Digging through old Windows versions on the Internet Archive, I found some early NT 3.1 pre-release versions that seemed promising, but the main issue seemed to be either incompatibility with today’s executable format or API changes that came later in development. The earliest 1991 versions used a draft PE format not compatible with modern Windows, and builds up to mid-1992 assumed the cdecl calling convention instead of stdcall for Windows API calls, so arguments would get removed twice, as such: push hwnd ; 4 bytes of args call [ShowWindow] ; Win11 ShowWindow is stdcall, ends with "ret 4" and removes them add esp, 4 ; the 1992 caller removes them again Which would understandably cause the program to crash. There was one application that caught my eye though, from Build 347, and that was CDPLAYER.EXE , linked on 16-Nov-1992 . By then the calling convention was fixed, but the other programs in that build crash in their bundled C runtime. CDPLAYER.EXE avoids that by using the system’s crtdll.dll , and Windows 11 still ships a crtdll.dll in SysWOW64 . If you start the program, you get something like this: That is because, duh, my computer doesn’t have a CD-ROM drive. But you can use a small DLL ( cdemu.dll ) to emulate one with some fake audio data and actually get it to play audio: Pretty cool for a program that’s almost 34 years old! What if we cheat? So earlier I mentioned that 16-bit programs are out of the picture because they are no longer supported. But if you want, you can use something like otvdm to run older Windows applications. Behold, a fully playable version of REVERSI.EXE dated 15-N
articles.oneLineKo: Windows 11에서 구동되는 가장 오래된 GUI 앱 찾기
articles.summaryKo: 저자는 Windows 11에서 수정이나 에뮬레이션 없이 실행되는 가장 오래된 GUI 애플리케이션을 찾는 탐구를 진행했다. 1993년 2월 날짜의 FREECELL.EXE가 작동함을 확인했지만, 더 오래된 것을 찾기 위해 Internet Archive의 초기 NT 3.1 프리릴리스 버전들을 조사했다. 1991년 버전은 PE 포맷 비호환, 1992년 중반까지는 cdecl/stdcall 호출 규약 불일치로 실행이 불가능했으며, 결국 1992년 11월 빌드의 CDPLAYER.EXE가 crtdll.dll 덕분에 정상 작동함을 발견했다. 16비트 프로그램은 NTVDM 부재로 기본 실행이 불가능하지만 otvdm 같은 도구로 REVERSI.EXE 등을 에뮬레이션해 실행할 수 있음도 언급했다.
